To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BMI is a strong predictor of outcome in patients admitted to hospital with ACS, and obese patients have the best outcomes.
obese ACS patients have the lowest in-hospital mortality compared to other BMI groups and the most obese have the highest in-hospital mortality.
In a large contemporary ACS cohort, BMI was associated with outcomes in a U shaped relationship.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between obesity and cardiovascular outcomes.
the impact of obesity and overweight on the health of people with cardiovascular disease (CVD), and in particular the impact on the risk of death.
the relationship between body mass index and outcomes following an acute coronary syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BMI is an important risk factor in ACS and should be taken into consideration when managing patients.
obesity is not a bad thing in ACS patients.
obesity is associated with improved outcomes in ACS but only up to a threshold of 30 39 kg/m2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BMI is associated with all cause and CV mortality in an ACS, and that there may be a threshold effect.
BMI is an important predictor of outcomes following ACS, but the relationship between BMI and outcome is not linear.
BMI is associated with outcomes following an ACS, but the obesity paradox may not extend to the morbidly obese, who may in fact be at increased risk of adverse outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
obesity does not appear to be protective in the setting of an ACS, and the obesity paradox should be interpreted with caution.
BMI should be taken into account when managing patients post ACS, and that there is an optimal range of BMI for patients to achieve to maximise survival following an ACS.

BMI should not be used as the only marker of obesity, and that the obesity paradox may be a misnomer, as it is not a paradox at all, but rather a reflection of the fact that BMI is a poor measure of obesity.
